### page_1
Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC. (1979) 58, 769-184
Resolution of superimposed magnetizations in the
Devonian John O'Groats Sandstone, North Scotland
K. M. Storetvedt
Department of Geophysics, University of western Ontario,
London, Ontario N6A 5B7, Canada, and Department of Geophysics,
University of Bergen, 5014 Bergen, Norway
c .M . Carmichael
Department of Geophysics, University of Western Ontario,
London. Ontario N6A 5B7, Canada
Received 1979 February 1; in original form 1978 September 25
Summary. The John O'Groats Sandstone, on the north-east tip of Scotland,
is the uppermost unit of a thick Old Red Sandstone sequence from the
uppermost Middle Devonian. Samples from 13 sites have been treated by
thermal and acid leaching techniques making use of the convergence of re-
magnetization circles when stable end points were not reached. In some cases,
in which the magnetic constituents were asymmetrically distributed, splitting
the specimens proved useful. Two axes of magnetization have been identified.
The easiest to determine, called the A axis, is present most frequently in the
reversed sense, at roughly Dec 190°, Inc - 40". The normal component can
also be detected as stable end points on acid leaching. The A-axis
magnetization is carried mainly by the pigmented cement. The B axis, which
is aligned NNE-SSW and almost horizontal, is less well defined. Both the
A- and B-axis orientations cited are after making corrections for structural
tilts that are present at some of the sites. The direction of the B-axis
magnetization agrees well with that of other Devonian units from west of
the Great Glen Fault and is interpreted as having been acquired during, or
shortly after, deposition. The A magnetization is interpreted as having been
acquired during the Mesozoic, probably associated with regional burial and
subsequent tectonic uplift of the area during the Jurassic. Later tectonic
movements to produce at least the major structural tilts post-date the A
magnetization and may be related to crustal unrest at the opening of the
modern Atlantic. The John O'Groats directions are compatible with similar
directions found in the hncansby Neck, a volcanic vent that penetrates the
Sandstone.
1 Introduction
The geology of Caithness (Fig. 1) is characterized by a thick succession of Old Red Sand-
stone sediments. At the base of the sequence there are barren red mudstones, arkoses and

conglomerates which Westoll (1951) believed to be of Lower Old Red Sandstone age. The
overlying Caithness Flagstone constitutes the predominant lithological group and has a rich
Middle Old Red Sandstone fish fauna (Crampton & Carruthers 1914; Jarvik 1948; Westoll
1951). In north-east Caithness the Flagstone group is overlain by the John O’Groats Sand-
stone whose age, based on fish remains in a few thin horizons, has been regarded as upper-
most Middle Devonian (Crampton & Carruthers 1914; Phemister 1960; Donovan, Foster &
Westoll 1974).
A palaeomagnetic reconnaissance study by Stubbs (1958) showed that the untreated
NRM of the Caithness sediments, in spite of a considerable scatter, were basically reversely
magnetized. Waage & Storetvedt (1 973), who continued the palaeomagnetic study of
Caithness sediments by applying thermal demagnetization, found that the red strata near the
base of the sequence contained at least two superimposed magnetizations of opposite
polarity. However, the blocking temperature spectra were such that single component
remanences were extremely difficult to isolate. More recent investigations (Tarling et al.
1976; Turner, Vaughan & Tarling 1978) have emphasized the remagnetization aspects of
these rocks. Unfortunately the lacustrine units studied by Turner et al. (1978) contained
sulphides which decomposed on heating and prevented the use of the thermal demagnetiza-
tion technique above c. 6OO0C, which is the temperature range in which the magnetic carrier
of these rocks would most likely be haematite.
In the present paper we report on the experimental work that has been undertaken to
determine the magnetization history of the John O’Groats Sandstone. This study is closely
related to the work on the Duncansby Neck (cf: Fig. l), a volcanic plug that penetrates the
John O’Groats Sandstone (Storetvedt et al. 1978).
2 Sampling and laboratory procedures
The rock collection comprises block samples taken from 13 sites (numbered 1-1 1 and
14-15) along coastal sections between Gills Bay and Skirza Head (Fig. 1). The collected
material consists dominantly of fine-grained red sandstones; exceptions are site 15 which

Resolution of magnetizations in Scotland 77 1
represents the yellow sandstone in the lower part of the sequence and sites 1-3 which are
fairly calcareous. Further collection details are given in Table 1.
About 100 specimens in the form of cylinders 1.9 cm in both length and diameter have
been subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization in a furnace in which cooling to room
temperature takes place in a field of less than 10 nT. About 40 specimens were chemically
demagnetized in concentrated hydrochloric acid (10 N). In order to speed up the leaching
process the cylinders were perforated by using a diamond drill-bit of 8 mm diameter and
1 mm wall thickness (Morris & Carmichael 1978). In conjunction with the leaching treat-
ment many of the specimens were cut into halves, perpendicular to their axis, and studied
separately. After each demagnetization step the remanence parameters of each specimen
was measured using an astatic, a Digico or a Schonstedt DSM-1 magnetometer.

3 Decomposition of the NRM
Sites 1-3 and 15, where the material is more calcareous or yellow in colour, have not
given results that can be used for palaeomagnetic interpretation. These rocks either become
too weakly magnetic after a few demagnetization steps or their magnetic moments changed
erratically both on thermal and on leaching treatment.
Material from all the remaining sites behaves in a more systematic way; the specimens
either show stable end-point magnetization or they exhibit more or less systematic vectoral
swings as demagnetization progresses. Some of the swinging specimens move along well-
defined great circle paths, suggesting that the remanence is dominantly a two-component
system, but in other cases the directional variations are more complex. On the whole,
chemical demagnetization, combined with specimen slicing, has been able to extract more
detailed information from individual specimens than the thermal method. Chemically
treated specimens could be measured reproducibly down to lower intensity levels than could
thermally treated ones, the minimum intensities used are 1 x and 5 x 10-4A/m
respectively. Because of difference in the extent of demagnetization obtained by the two
methods Figs 2-5 show more results from the leaching procedure than from the thermal
treatment. These figures show interesting examples of multi-component magnetization in
several specimens. Only those which are regarded to have achieved a stable magnetization are
included in Table 2.

The most important magnetization axis in the John O’Groats Sandstone is directed
roughly north-south with an intermediately steep inclination. This axis of magnetization
will be referred to as the A axis. The reversed A magnetization (c. 190, -40) is the pre-
dominant one. The remanence direction in many specimens remain stationary in this
position over the major range of demagnetization, particularly on thermal treatment. It is
frequently found, however, that when demagnetizing the last 10 to 15 per cent of the
magnetic moment the remanence vector moves along a great circle path (cf: JO 25-A3 of
Fig. 3(b)). There are only a few specimens in this study for which the normalA magnetiza-
tion is defined by an end-point on demagnetization and only the chemical method has been
successful in isolating these end points. Specimen JO42-A1 (Fig, 2) is an example of a
specimen that reaches the normalA component. It is a general observation in this study that
the red pigment disappears relatively quickly and even in the most resistant specimens it is
completely removed in less than 200 hr of leaching. Also, the remanence intensity decays
rapidly in the initial stages of HC1 treatment. Removal of the pigment is in general connected
with a moving away of the remanence vector from the reversed A-axis position. It is con-
cluded, therefore, that the reversed A magnetization must be carried by the red iron-oxide
pigment while the normal A -axis component is associated with larger magnetic grains.
Fig. 3 illustrates two cases, JO 18-A1 and JO41-C1, where specimen slicing seems to
provide very useful information on within-specimen magnetization. JO 18-A1 starts out in
the reversed A-axis position and moves slowly but perfectly along a great circle path. After
158 hr of leaching the specimen was cut. On continued demagnetization the two smaller
specimens define remagnetization trends that are differently oriented compared to that of
the combined specimen and the three extended remagnetization circles intersect in the
position of the normal A-axis component. In palaeomagnetic studies one often encounters
specimens like JO41-C1 (Fig. 3(b)) which on demagnetization remain in a discordant
position. After 480 hr of leaching, which had reduced the remanence intensity by 85 per
cent, the specimen was cut. The two halves (x andy) define separate stable directions which,
together with the pre-cut magnetization, are distributed along a great circle that passes
through the A-axis components. In this case leaching removes the components at an equal
rate but fortunately the two components are not homogeneously distributed throughout the
volume of the specimen so that the composite nature of its remanence can be detected by
specimen slicing.
The second axis of magnetization in this formation, the B axis, is nearly horizontal and
strikes NNE-SSW. This magnetization is much less distinct than the A magnetization and
for its detection chemical treatment is a much more powerful technique than thermal

magnetization while the lower half was normally magnetized closer to the A axis. Further
leaching up to 344 hr did not change these directions significantly. It is important to

associated with intensity increases (see Fig. 4(e)). There is of course no guarantee that the
specimen split provide clearly separated sub-components so JO 70-A2 may either contain
the two Baxis components or, alternatively, the normal A vector plus the reversed B
magnetization. Specimen JO46-A1 (Fig. 5(b)) has also an uneven distribution of its
magnetizations. Thus the upper half, which carries the bulk of the intensity, is discordantly

4 Palaeomagnetic results
Sixty specimens tend to give stable magnetic directions. Of these about 70 per cent had
stable magnetizations throughout the complete demagnetization range, or reached end
points upon thermal and/or chemical demagnetization. For the latter group the terminal
directions were mostly defined by the mean of three or more demagnetization steps.
Exceptions are a few specimens, the results of which are given in brackets in Table 2, that
seem to define characteristic directions of magnetization for the formation but where the
'stable' end points are based on two steps only (on continued demagnetization the moment
became too low for reliable measurement). The remaining 30 per cent had stable directions
of magnetization until less than 10 per cent of their original intensity remained and then
their directions changed in an erratic and non-reproducible manner. For these the stable

data for the 60 specimens are listed in Table 2. There were 31 additional specimens whose
directions moved along paths directed generally to the north but which did not reach stable
end points before their intensity fell below the level of reproducible measurement. The
data for these specimens are not included in Table 2 but were used for the great circle
analyses (see below) which yields the poles given as A* and B* in Table 3. Attempts at
vector subtraction for this latter group of specimens did not prove successful in finding the
reversed sub-components which suggests that their component magnetizations have too
much overlap of their stability spectra.
The sedimentary strata at the different collecting sites dip at various angles up to about
45' (see Table 1). To determine the timing of this tectonic tilting relative to the time of
magnetization, the directions of all those specimens from Table 2 having intermediate to
steep inclinations, i.e. those interpreted as defining the A axis, were plotted before and after
tectonic corrections. This plot is shown in Fig. 6 in which plot a is before, and plot b is after,

tectonic corrections. Making the correction produces a marked improvement toward a two-

in the column headed Group in Table 2, and by an V over their symbol in Fig. 6(b), which
do not fall into the grouping. This may be due to some part of their magnetization being
acquired after tilting or to unresolved components of magnetization. Whatever the cause of
their anomalous directions of magnetization these specimens have been excluded in the
calculation of the A-axis pole position given in Table 3. The reduced scatter of the grouping
by the tectonic correction indicates that at least the major part of the structural dip of the
John O'Groats Sandstone post-dates the A magnetization. Since the A component is
interpreted as being the younger of the two characteristic magnetizations (see below), all
the results of this study have been subjected to tectonic correction.
The reversed group of Fig. qb) has a certain elongation that may be caused by improper
structural correction; for example that a minor part of the tilting may pre-date the A
magnetization or alternatively the unfolding to the palaeo-horizontal may be more complex
than simple rotation of bedding about present strike direction. In Fig. 7 the magnetization
directions of the specimens are plotted as though they all had reverse polarity to separate
them on the diagram from the location of the intersection points of northward trending
remagnetization circles. The directional trends plotted here are only those which lie along

Overall palaeomagnetic results are listed in Table 3. There is very good agreement
between the mean direction of the reversed A group (Table 2 data) and the corresponding
best intersection point of the remagnetization trends. The B magnetization is of subordinate
importance compared to the A magnetization. Only 12 specimen directions define this axis.
The normal intersection point of directional trends agrees well with the characteristic
directions derived from an independent sample population although this convergence point
is much more ill-defined than that of the A axis. The angular difference between the mean
A and B magnetizations is c. 50’ and the mean directions are significantly different at the
95 per cent probability level.
5 Magnetic mineralogy
The magnetic mineralogy of the John O’Groats Sandstone samples is quite different from
that of the lacustrine units further down in the Caithness Old Red Sandstone section that
were investigated by Turner et al. (1978). These authors found magnetite and relatively large
amounts of iron sulphide that oxidized upon heating to produce a magnetically very soft
component which was probably additional magnetite. This soft component picked up
spurious magnetizations in the laboratory and prevented thermal demagnetization at
temperatures that would have determined any natural remanence carried by haematite.
In contrast to the Turner et al. (1978) lacustrine units, the natural remanence of the
John O’Groats samples is carried exclusively in various haematite phases. These can be
divided into two categories, haematite in relatively large sedimentary grains and haematite
in the cementing matrix.
Considering the large-grain category first, these are interpreted optically as being
originally iron titanium oxides in both a spinel form, i.e. titanomagnetite, and a rhombo-
hedral form, i.e. ilmenite. Both of these forms have been severely oxidized to haematite
and rutile. Grains that are inferred to have been titanomagnetite originally are roughly

### page_12
780 K. M. Storetvedt and C. M. Gamichael
equidimensional in shape and have the crystal axes of the haematite phases aligned along 11 1
directions. None of the original magnetite has survived. An example of this type of grain is
shown in Plate l(b). Grains inferred to have been ilmenite originally are elongated in shape
and have separated into irregular areas of variable reflectivity without any particular
alignment of the crystal axes of these areas. Otherwise they are similar in appearance to
Plate l(b). In all of the samples a proportion of the large grains has been completely
converted to rutile. This proportion varies in different samples from around 40 to 100 per
cent. To convert the grains to rutile would require not only oxidation but also some process,
such as attack by acidic solutions, to remove the iron. Attack by acidic solutions is suggested
because the large grains that are now rutile in the natural samples are indistinguishable from
all the large grains in samples that have been completely leached in hydrochloric acid. An
example of a large grain that is mostly rutile but still has some haematite at the centre is
(a). shown in Plate l(c) and The timing of the alteration of the large grains would be after
deposition, because the rutile end product is no longer a coherent grain and could not be
deposited in that form, but before the red cement was introduced because haematitic
staining of the cement would be much more vulnerable to the acid solution than the larger
grains would be.
The haematite associated with the cementing matrix is present in several forms. Particle
sizes of haematite large enough to reflect light have developed throughout most of the
cement as scattered dust and also as veins and rims of some sediment particles (Plate l(e)).
All of the haematite associated with the cement is in small enough particles to show ruby red
translucence when viewed with crossed polarizers. Included in the haematite associated with
the red cement is some that has formed as an alteration product of sedimentary grains.
These seem to have been altered during the cementing process since they are now only relict
structures within the cementing matrix (Plate l(f)). The haematitic staining of the cement
may not contribute to the magnetization. This conclusion comes from examination of those
samples that had initial moments of the order of 1 x 10-3A/m and thus were too weak to
apply the demagnetization techniques even though they have abundant red staining of the
cement (see C of Plate l(a)). These were samples from sites 2 and 3 of Table 1. In all of
them the original large grains had been converted to rutile and there are very few haematite
particles large enough to reflect light. Microscopic examination of polished thin sections of
samples at various stages of the acid leaching process show clearly that the haematite
associated with the cementing matrix is destroyed more rapidly than are the larger grains.
Since the acid attacks the larger grains within volumes of the sample from which the
haematite in the cement has been removed, however, part of the magnetization carried by
the large grains will be destroyed before all of that carried by the cement is removed. The
technique of making drill cuts in the samples, which is illustrated in Plate l(a), minimizes
this overlapping in the demagnetization process by allowing rapid penetration of the acid to
the interior of the sample. Because of the observed order in which the haematite is removed
in the leaching process it is concluded that the more resistant B-axis magnetization is carried
by some of the larger grains. The A axis is inferred to be carried by the haematite associated
with cementing matrix as well as by some of the larger grains that probably suffered further
oxidation during the cementing process. This association of the two axes of magnetization
with the different categories of haematite is supported by examination of sample JO 41 in
which the B axis predominates (Fig. 4(a)). It contains many large grains in which there is
little or no alteration to rutile and the red cement contains less polishable haematite.
Thermal demagnetization curves, such as those shown in Figs 2(d) and 3(d), show the
presence of components that unblock over temperature ranges usually found for magnetite.
There is no evidence of magnetite being present, however, because none is observed in

These are now only relict structures outlined by the haematite decoration.

Resolution of magnetizations in Scotland 78 1
polished section and negligible moment is induced in the samples in magnetic fields up to
800 mT. These lower temperature unblocking components are interpreted as being a
combination of the effect of small particle size among the haematite grains in the cement
and titanium in the haematite formed in the altered large grains. The relatively high degree
of optical anisotropy of the haematite in grains such as the one shown in Plate l(b) suggest
considerable Ti content. Such causes for the distribution of unblocking temperatures would
account for the general poorer success in separating the A and B components by the thermal
demagnetization technique as compared to the acid leaching procedure.
6 Magnetization history
The palaeomagnetic results outlined above agree very well with recent palaeomagnetic
findings in the Duncansby volcanic vent (Storetvedt et al. 1978). This small basic intrusion
which cuts through the John O’Groats Sandstone is shown to possess a two-axis magnetiza-
tion: the palaeomagnetically oldest axis corresponds extremely well with Old Red Sandstone
data from Caithness and Orkney (Storetvedt & Petersen 1972; Waage & Storetvedt 1973)
while the second axis seems related to a Mesozoic overprinting event (cf: Fig. 8). It has been
concluded therefore (Storetvedt et al. 1978) that the Duncansby Neck most likely relates
to the volcanism at the base of the Upper Old Red Sandstone in the nearby Island of Hoy
(Halliday, McAlpine & Mitchell 1977).
As seen from Fig. 8 the John O’Groats B pole plots in agreement with other Old Red
Sandstone poles from west of the Great Glen Fault. These poles have about a 15’ longi-
tudinal displacement to the left of the corresponding position for stable continental Europe.
The John O’Groats results are thus compatible with the proposition that there is a
discordance in Old Red Sandstone palaeomagnetism across the Great Glen Fault which has
been associated with a major sinistral trans-current movement along this dislocation
(Storetvedt 1974,1975).
The A pole plots in a Mesozoic position relative to the European polar wander curve. A
reliable assessment of the age of this magnetization overprint is hampered by an incomplete
knowledge of Mesozoic palaeomagnetism for Europe. However, carefully tested data from
suggested late Jurassic-Cretaceous volcanics from Spitsbergen (poles 10 and 11 of Fig. 8)
suggest a marked eastward polar migration for Europe that is fully compatible with
corresponding observations from North America. It is thought, therefore, that the Mesozoic
polar curve suggested in Fig. 8 is essentially correct. On these assumptions the John O’Groats
A pole can probably be assigned an age of around Lower-Middle Jurassic.
The strong Mesozoic magnetization overprint appears to be a general phenomenon in
Old Red Sandstone rocks from Caithness (Storetvedt et al. 1978; Turner et al. 1978).
Following the concept outlined in Storetvedt et al. (1978), in which this problem has been
discussed at some length, it is suggested that the coastal districts of north-east Scotland
formed part of the North Sea depositional basin in late Palaeozoic and early Mesozoic
times. This provided a lengthy burial history for the Old Red Sandstone strata giving rise to
a temperature elevation that enhanced chemical processes as well as increasing the rate at
which viscous magnetization would be acquired. The secondary magnetization of the
Duncansby Neck (Storetvedt et al. 1978) was interpreted as having been frozen in as a
result of uplift during a period of regional tectonic unrest in the Lower-Middle Jurassic. As
a result of this tectonic activity along the Great Glen Fault and in the Moray Firth basin
(Bacon & Chesher 1975) the Jurassic sediments are down-faulted relative to the Old Red
Sandstone sediments exposed on the landward side. Similar features are also exposed
onshore along the Helmsdale Fault.

Figure 8. The John O’Groats poles A and B seen in conjunction with the suggested European polar
wander path for part of Phanerozoic time. Poles 1,5,6 and 9 are mean poles from the following sources:
1 = Storetvedt (1967); 5, 6 and 9 = Phillips & Forsyth (1972) (other sources give similar results). Poles
from individual formations are as follows: 2 = Waage & Storetvedt (1973); 3 = Storetvedt & Petersen
(1972); 7 = Zijderveld (1975); 10 = Briseid & Halvorsen (1974); 11 = Sandal & Halvorsen (1973). Poles
4 and 8 are for the Duncansby Neck which intrudes the John O’Groats Sandstone (Storetvedt et al.
1978). Poles A,B ,a nd B, are for the John O’Groats Sandstone and are taken from Table 3.
The Mesozoic magnetization overprint in the Duncansby Neck (pole 8 of Fig. 8) has a
more westerly, i.e. probably older, pole position than that of the corresponding John
O’Groats magnetization. This may reflect differences in the mode of acquisition of the
secondary magnetizations. The Duncansby overprint is seen as a viscous remanence
impressed during burial at elevated temperatures. The John O’Groats overprint is associated
with fine haematite grains in the red cementing matrix. This material has unblocking
temperatures ranging well above 600°C and clearly in excess of those associated with the
demagnetization of the Duncansby Neck. It is unlikely, however, that the magnetization of
the red cement has been acquired during cooling from such high temperatures: it is more
probable that it is a CRM acquired as the haematite formed in the cement by a de-
hydration-oxidation process. If this process continued to temperatures lower than those
required partly to remagnetize the Duncansby Neck, then the A magnetization of the John
O’Groats Sandstone could have been acquired at a later state of the uplift process. This
could explain the different pole positions for the secondary magnetizations of the two rock
types.
The removal upon tilt correction of the majority of discordant, mostly steeply inclined,
directions of magnetization suggest that at least the major tectonic phase, having affected
the John O’Groats Sandstone, must be of post-Lower-Middle Jurassic age. This is likely to
be connected with the crustal unrest that preceded the formation of the modern North
Atlantic.
7 Conclusions
We conclude that the John O’Groats Sandstone acquired its oldest magnetization component
during or shortly after deposition in Middle-Upper Devonian time. A subsequent large-
scale transcurrent movement along the Great Glen Fault (probably in the uppermost
Downloaded

### page_16
Resolution of magnetizations in Scotland 783
Devonian) led to a slight clockwise rotation of the north-west part of Scotland west of the
Great Glen Fault. In subsequent times the coastal districts of north Scotland became part
of the North Sea depositional basin and the Old Red Sandstone strata of Caithness, including
the John O'Groats sequence, were buried under a pile of Upper Palaeozoic and Lower
Mesozoic sediments of unknown thickness. This burial led to a rise in temperature resulting
in an enhancement of thermo-chemical magnetization processes. Thus, at about the
TriassiclJurassic boundary the original palaeomagnetism had been nearly completely erased.
A strong Mesozoic overprint was subsequently frozen in as a result of the uplift connected
with the important volcano-tectonic phase that affected the northern North Sea in Lower-
Middle Jurassic time. The acquisition of the secondary magnetization is therefore tied into
the regional geological framework. At some time after uplift the John O'Groats Sandstone
was affected by a structural deformation causing stratal dips ranging upwards to about
45O:This event is thought to be related to final continental breakup and initiation of sea-
floor spreading in the North Atlantic.
